awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I:  High-Throughput AST Using Gradient-Based Microfluidic
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is to create a rapid point-of-care antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) kit that can be run on the same day the sample is taken. This will help physicians to utilize the best antibiotic at the optimal dosage sooner, reducing the number of exposures for antimicrobial resistance (AMR).  Such infections are responsible for more than 2.8 million infections and 35,000 deaths annually in the U.S. The integration of the proposed platform with mobile devices for result interpretation ensures that it can be widely deployed, including in resource-limited settings and during emergencies. This adoptability is crucial for promptly responding to future pandemics and ensuring that even remote or underserved areas have access to advanced diagnostic capabilities. This project will help to reduce the economic burden associated with AMR ($20 billion/year) and infectious diseases ($41 billion/year). Once commercialized, the proposed platform is expected to promote better antibiotic stewardship, reducing antibiotic release into the environment. Antibiotics in plants and the food chain pose risks to human and animal health, and contribute to the spread of resistant bacteria, making infections harder to treat and increasing outbreak risk.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will develop a novel microfluidic platform for rapid and precise AST. Current methods, such as broth microdilution and Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion, are limited by long turnaround times of 3-5 days. This delay leads to a postponement in adjusting antibiotics. Even emerging rapid diagnostic systems, while quicker, still require >20 hours to provide results, resulting in >4 doses of broad-spectrum antibiotics before precision adjustments can be made. The proposed platform generates actionable results within 6-9 hours from time of sample, as opposed to the conventional 3-5 days, identifying not only the most efficacious drug but also the appropriate dose. In the short-term, the technology will improve patient outcomes, particularly in life-threatening conditions like sepsis. In the long-term, more precise antibiotic usage promotes stewardship and extends the overall value we can derive from antibiotics before resistance mechanisms become ubiquitous. Three primary areas of risk will be addressed during this project: 1. Compatibility with scalable manufacturing materials used in injection molding, 2. Extending the shelf life to >6 months by lyophilizing pre-loaded antibiotics, and 3. Creating colorimetric interpretation software that can run on mobile devices to provide accessible and objective analysis and readouts.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcomes Report

NSF Award #2444168 — SBIR Phase I: High-Throughput Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing Using Gradient-Based Microfluidics

Antimicrobial resistance is among the most serious public health threats facing the United States. More than 2.8 million antimicrobial-resistant infections occur here each year, causing over 35,000 deaths and more than $20 billion in direct medical costs. Sepsis is the most expensive condition treated in U.S. hospitals, and a patient's chance of survival declines with each hour that passes before effective antibiotic therapy begins.

When a patient arrives with a serious infection, clinicians face a timing problem. The laboratory test that determines which antibiotics will actually work—antimicrobial susceptibility testing—requires 16 to 24 hours after a bacterial isolate becomes available and several days from when the patient's sample is collected. Because treatment cannot wait, physicians begin broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately and adjust only after results return, typically after several doses have been given. That interval of broad-spectrum use is a major driver of resistance, of side effects, and of avoidable cost.

This Phase I project developed a disposable microfluidic test cartridge that shortens the susceptibility test itself from 16-24 hours to 3-4 hours and that runs on laboratory instruments hospitals already own.

The cartridge generates a continuous range of antibiotic concentrations through controlled diffusion. An antibiotic introduced at one end spreads into an array of tiny isolated chambers, each ending up with a slightly different concentration. Bacteria placed in the cartridge reveal whether they are growing through a color-changing dye that responds to living cells. The lowest concentration that stops growth is the answer clinicians need. Because each chamber holds less than a millionth of a liter, results appear far faster than in conventional formats.

The project had three technical goals, all of which were met.

The first was to build the device from a plastic suitable for mass manufacturing. Earlier prototypes used a rubber-like material that lets trapped air escape through its walls, convenient in the laboratory but not manufacturable at scale. Manufacturable plastics do not breathe, and trapped air ruins the test. The team designed and tested twenty-one successive versions before arriving at a design that reliably clears air from every chamber, confirmed against five separate quality measures.

The second was shelf life. The team freeze-dried the cartridge contents so they can be stored dry at room temperature without refrigeration. The result went beyond what was proposed: rather than drying the antibiotic alone, the team dried the entire test chemistry into the cartridge, so a user adds only the bacteria. Cartridges held at 50°C with daily temperature swings for six months, far harsher than normal storage or shipping, produced no serious errors at any point.

The third was a readout requiring no new equipment. The original plan was a smartphone camera application. Conversations with clinical laboratory directors changed that plan: every laboratory consulted already owned microplate readers, and directors said a smartphone-based result would not be accepted in regulated clinical workflows. The cartridge was therefore designed to fit directly into standard plate readers, requiring no adapter and no modification.

Performance was measured against the reference laboratory method using clinical bacterial strains from the CDC & FDA Antimicrobial Resistance Isolate Bank—real drug-resistant organisms rather than laboratory strains. Across 120 test comparisons covering four bacterial species responsible for much of hospital-acquired infection and sepsis, results agreed with the reference method 95.8 percent of the time, with zero errors of the most dangerous type, in which a resistant organism is incorrectly reported as treatable.

The project also produced an unplanned result. The same cartridge, with one minor dimensional change, correctly identified drug resistance in three species of Candida, a fungus that causes serious bloodstream infections. Antifungal testing is comparatively underserved by rapid diagnostic technology, and this finding indicates the approach is not limited to bacteria.

The company advanced commercially and toward regulatory review during the award. GIANT BioSystems closed a $250,000 SAFE investment led by Draper Associates and added a VP of Clinical Affairs with prior responsibility for clinical microbiology operations at a major health system. A pre-submission meeting with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration established the regulatory pathway and the evidence a gradient-based test will need. Informed by that discussion, the company's initial development focus is a Gram-negative bacterial panel, with additional organism groups to follow.

The broader significance of this work is timing and access. A result available in a few hours rather than a day changes when a physician can narrow antibiotic therapy, reducing both the resistance pressure and the side effects of unnecessary broad-spectrum use. Because the test requires no dedicated instrument, no refrigeration, and no reagent preparation, it suits smaller hospitals and laboratories that cannot justify specialized equipment and potentially settings without reliable cold storage.

Work continues toward expanded clinical validation, manufacturing scale-up, and regulatory review.
